input: The separation under consideration is a binary distillation of ethanol and water, for which the relative volatility has a value of 1.53 and is taken, for the purposes of the calculation, to remain constant throughout the column. The product specifications call for a distillate containing 98 mol% of the light component and bottoms containing 2 mol% of the light component. Application of the Fenske relation yields a minimum stage count of 18.3 theoretical stages, the reboiler being included in the count. It should be appreciated that the Fenske figure corresponds to operation at total reflux, under which no product is withdrawn and the entire internal traffic is available for the separation; the figure accordingly represents a lower bound on the number of stages that any real column will require in order to achieve the specified split, since a column operated at a finite reflux ratio will invariably need additional stages. The assumption of constant relative volatility is what permits the minimum count to be evaluated directly from the end compositions and the volatility. In the actual design, a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum value has been adopted. The number of stages required at this operating reflux cannot be obtained from the Fenske relation itself, which furnishes the count only in the total-reflux limit, and it has instead been obtained from a separate simulation of the column.
target: A binary distillation separates ethanol and water at a relative volatility of 1.53, taken as constant over the column. The specifications are a distillate of 98 mol% light component and bottoms of 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 18.3 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. The Fenske count is the stage count at total reflux, where no product is withdrawn and the whole separation is driven by the internal traffic. It is a lower bound on the stages that any operating column needs for the stated split. A column run at finite reflux needs more stages than the minimum, because part of the traffic that total reflux spends on separation is withdrawn as product. The constant relative volatility is the assumption that lets the count be computed from the two end compositions and the volatility alone. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum. At that reflux the stage count comes from a separate simulation, not from the Fenske relation: the relation gives the count only at total reflux, and the minimum reflux only at an infinite count, so neither operating quantity follows from it. The two design quantities are therefore fixed by different routes. The minimum count also disciplines the simulation: a simulated stage count below the Fenske minimum for the same split would contradict the total-reflux bound and would point to an error in the simulation rather than to a discovery about the column.
